passage: Chetan and Asif stood on the old bridge over the canal outside their village. The water was brown and fast after the rain. "Dare you to jump," Asif said, grinning. Chetan looked down. His legs felt weak. "No, yaar. Too fast. I'm not jumping." Asif laughed. "Scared?" "Yes. And you'd have to carry me home in a bucket." Asif laughed harder. "Okay, okay." "Race you to the banyan tree instead?" They ran off together.

qa.q: What did Asif dare Chetan to do?
qa.a: Asif dared him to jump from the old bridge into the canal.

qa.q: What does Chetan's weak legs suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt afraid and knew the jump was dangerous.

qa.q: How did Chetan refuse without losing the friendship?
qa.a: He said no honestly, used a joke, and suggested a safer game instead.

qa.q: How might Asif see Chetan's refusal?
qa.a: Asif may respect him more for being honest and funny, and still want to play with him.

grounding: It shows a child refusing a risky dare while keeping the friendship.

passage: On their street in Lisbon, Javier pointed at a blue door. "The old lady there gets so angry. Let's ring her bell and run." Tomas hesitated. He remembered the lady giving them oranges last summer. "Nah. She's nice. She'd get scared." "Come on, it's just a joke." "It's not funny for her," Tomas said. He picked up his skateboard. "Let's go to the ramps." Javier rolled his eyes, then followed.

qa.a: It was a blue door.

qa.q: What might Tomas have been thinking when he hesitated?
qa.a: He remembered the lady's kindness and didn't want to scare or upset her.

qa.q: How might the old lady be affected if they rang and ran?

passage: In the girls' hostel, Kunal's sister had passed on a note: "Sneak out tonight? Kunal and his friends are going to the night market." Shalini's roommate squealed. Shalini frowned. The gate was locked at nine, and the road was dark. "No, I'm not going." "Don't be boring!" At breakfast, Kunal teased her. "Scaredy cat." Shalini shrugged. "I like my bed. Tell me what you ate." He laughed, and they shared the samosas he'd brought back.

qa.a: The gate was locked at nine.

qa.q: What does Shalini's frown suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and was weighing the risks of sneaking out.

qa.q: How did Shalini keep the friendship with Kunal?
qa.a: She said no calmly, didn't lecture him, and stayed friendly at breakfast.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Shalini after she refuses?
qa.a: He teases her but still shares samosas, suggesting he respects her choice.

grounding: It shows a child refusing an unsafe request in a hostel without losing the friendship.

passage: I'm Ritu, Zubin's cousin; I was visiting that week. The colony boys were bored on the terrace. Then someone said, 'Zubin, throw a stone at the Sharmas' dog. Bet you can't hit it.' Everyone went 'Ooooh'. Zubin had a stone in his hand already, from their game. He looked at it for a long moment. I couldn't tell if he was scared or just thinking. Then he tossed it over his shoulder into the plant pot. 'Nah, it's old and it limps. Race you to the water tank instead. Loser buys ice golas.' The boys groaned, then ran. Zubin won. Nobody mentioned the dog again, and he was still captain the next day.

qa.q: What did the boys dare Zubin to do?
qa.a: They dared him to throw a stone at the Sharmas' dog.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been thinking during his long look at the stone?
qa.a: He may have been weighing the dare against hurting an old dog, though Ritu couldn't tell if he was scared or just thinking.

qa.q: Why did Zubin's way of saying no work so well?
qa.a: He refused lightly, gave a reason and offered a fun race instead, so the group had something else to do.

qa.q: What would have changed if Zubin had lectured the boys?
qa.a: They might have mocked him or done the dare themselves, and he could have lost his place in the group.

grounding: An observer sees a child refuse an unkind dare without losing his friends.

passage: Monday: Uday and the girls from the back row wanted Pallavi, twelve, to hide Meenal's new geometry box 'just for fun'. Pallavi laughed nervously and said, 'Maybe later,' and hated herself on the way home. Wednesday: Uday asked again, holding the box out to her. Pallavi's heart thumped. 'No. She saved for that. She'd cry.' Uday rolled his eyes. 'You're so boring.' 'Then play boring kho-kho with me at break.' He hesitated, then shrugged. 'Fine, but I'm chasing first.' Next Tuesday: The box stayed on Meenal's desk. At break, Uday yelled, 'Pallavi's on my team!' before anyone else could pick. She grinned and ran over.

qa.q: What game did Pallavi suggest instead of hiding the box?
qa.a: She suggested playing kho-kho at break.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel after saying 'Maybe later' on Monday?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of herself, because she had laughed nervously and dodged the unkind request instead of refusing it.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do on Wednesday that helped keep the friendship?
qa.a: She said a clear no with a reason and then invited Uday to play, so he wasn't pushed away.

qa.q: How might Meenal's week have gone if Pallavi had agreed?
qa.a: Meenal might have lost her new box that she saved for and felt hurt and picked on.

grounding: Over several days a child moves from dodging to clearly refusing an unkind request while keeping her friendship.

passage:
Jomon, you asked why I never climb trees with you boys anymore. Let your Farhan Nana tell you.
When I was eleven, in our village near Kannur, my friends dared me to jump from the high wall of the old well into the water. “Scared?” they shouted.
I was scared. The water was dark, and nobody knew how deep. My legs shook on the wall. But I climbed down.
“No,” I said. “Let's race to the mango tree instead. Loser buys ice sticks.”
They laughed. Some called me a coward. But they came to race.
The next summer, a boy from the next village jumped from that same wall and broke his leg. My friends never mentioned the word coward again.

qa.q: Where did the friends dare Farhan to jump from?
qa.a: From the high wall of the old well into the water.

qa.q: How did young Farhan feel on the wall?
qa.a: He felt scared, his legs shaking, unsure how deep the water was.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept Farhan safe and kept his friends?
qa.a: Saying no and suggesting a race instead, so he refused the dare without losing the friendship.

qa.q: How might the boy who broke his leg have felt?
qa.a: He was probably in pain and scared, maybe wishing he had said no too.

grounding: A grandfather recalls saying no to a dangerous dare and keeping his friends.

passage:
The power went off across the whole building, and the children were playing in the dark stairwell. Wasim said, “Dare you to go up to the terrace and stand on the water-tank ledge. In the dark.”
The others clapped. “Keerthana! Keerthana!”
Keerthana, eleven, felt her heart thump. The ledge had no railing.
“No,” she said. “Let's play torch-tag in the courtyard instead. I've got the torch.”
Wasim rolled his eyes, but when she switched the torch on, everyone followed her down.
At home, Keerthana told her mother about the dare. That same night her mother called the society secretary, who locked the terrace door before the power came back.

qa.q: What did Wasim dare Keerthana to do?
qa.a: To go up to the terrace and stand on the water-tank ledge in the dark.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when the others chanted her name?
qa.a: She felt nervous, her heart thumping, but she stayed firm.

qa.q: What made Keerthana's refusal work without losing her friends?
qa.a: She said no clearly and offered a fun alternative, torch-tag, that everyone could join.

qa.q: How did Keerthana's mother respond when told about the dare?
qa.a: She called the society secretary that same night, who locked the terrace door.

grounding: During a power cut an eleven-year-old refuses a dangerous dare, keeps her friends, and tells an adult who acts.

passage:
At the corner shop in their Kolkata lane, Anirban nudged Ramesh, twelve. “Dare you to put that chocolate in your pocket. Uncle won't see.”
Ramesh looked at the shopkeeper, bent over his accounts. His heart raced.
“No,” he said. “That's stealing. And Uncle gives us free toffees on Diwali.”
“You're boring.”
“Maybe.” Ramesh took out his coins, bought one chocolate and broke it in half. “Here. Boring chocolate.”
Anirban grinned and took it. “Okay, okay.”
They walked out together, eating.

qa.q: What did Anirban dare Ramesh to do?
qa.a: To put the chocolate in his pocket without paying.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel when Anirban dared him?

qa.q: How did Ramesh say no without losing the friendship?

qa.q: How might Anirban feel after Ramesh shares the chocolate?
qa.a: He probably feels a bit silly but happy, and their friendship stays strong.

grounding: A twelve-year-old refuses an unkind dare to steal and keeps the friendship.

passage:
"Climb the water tank ladder. Top rung. I dare you," said Farhan.
Karthik looked up. The ladder was rusty and very high.
"No way. It's dangerous."
"Scared?"
"Yes. And so should you be." Karthik grinned. "Race you to the ground instead. Loser buys the next bat."
Farhan hesitated. "You're boring."
"And alive."
Farhan laughed. "Fine. But I'm winning."
They ran. At home that evening, Karthik told his father about the rusty ladder. His father called the society secretary right away to have it chained.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he looked up at the ladder?
qa.a: Karthik felt scared and wary, knowing the climb was dangerous.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Karthik says "And alive"?
qa.a: Farhan probably feels amused and a bit relieved, since the joke let him drop the dare without losing face.

grounding: A child refuses a dangerous dare with humour and his father makes the ladder safe.

passage:
Last year, in Class 6, Pranav dared me to ring Mrs D'Souza's doorbell and run. She's old and walks with a stick.
"Everyone's done it," he said. "Don't be a baby."
I felt my face heat. I wanted to be brave. But I kept thinking of Mrs D'Souza getting up slowly, walking to the door, and finding nobody.
"No," I said. "That's mean to her."
Pranav rolled his eyes. For a day he didn't talk to me. Then he came over with his cricket bat like nothing had happened.
I'm Bhavna. I still wave to Mrs D'Souza every morning. She always waves back.

qa.q: Whose doorbell did Pranav dare Bhavna to ring?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza's.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when her face heated?
qa.a: Bhavna felt embarrassed and pressured, wanting to look brave in front of Pranav.

qa.q: What helped Bhavna say no?
qa.a: Thinking about how the dare would affect Mrs D'Souza made it clear that it was unkind.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt when Bhavna refused?
qa.a: Pranav was probably annoyed and embarrassed for a day, but still valued the friendship enough to come back.

grounding: A young person recalls refusing an unkind dare and keeping the friendship.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Thursday.
At lunch today, Kalyani dared Ritu to jump off the top of the school wall onto the sandpit. Ritu looked at the height, then said, "No. I'll break my leg. Let's do long jump on the ground instead."
Kalyani laughed and said, "Chicken!" Ritu didn't budge. She drew a line in the sand and said, "Beat me."
They ended up playing long jump for the rest of lunch.
Afterwards, Ritu came to me and told me about the dare. I thanked her. This afternoon I spoke to Kalyani and to the class about wall-jumping, and asked the caretaker to put up a sign. — Ms Nair

Today Nazia dared me to climb onto the water tank roof. Everyone was chanting my name. My legs were shaking.

Nazia is still my friend. She even said, "You were right, the ladder was wobbly."

During Diwali in their small town, older boys dared Suraj, ten, to hold a lit firecracker in his hand.
His friend Deepika said, "Don't do it."
Suraj wanted to look brave. His hand hovered. Then he pulled back. "No. I want to keep my fingers."
The boys laughed. Suraj and Deepika walked away and told his uncle, who came out at once, took the firecrackers from the boys, and sent them home.
Later Deepika said, "You're braver for saying no."
Suraj grinned.

On the way home, Kwame told his father about the dare. His father walked back with them before dark and warned the older kids' parents.
Gabriel said, "Okay. You were right."

In the monsoon, the drain behind the hostel dining hall became a rushing stream. After dinner, Gargi, Tarun's closest friend, pointed at it. "I dare you to jump across. Everyone's watching."
Tarun looked at the brown, fast water and felt his legs go weak. "No way. That's how people get swept off."
"Scaredy cat," someone said.
"Maybe. Still no." Tarun smiled at Gargi. "Race you to the common room instead? Loser does my laundry."
Gargi laughed and ran. On the way, Tarun stopped at the warden's office. "People are daring each other to jump the drain," he said. The warden went out at once, sent everyone inside, and put a rope and a sign across the path that night.
Gargi rolled her eyes. "Snitch." But she saved him a seat.

qa.q: What did the warden put across the path?
qa.a: The warden put a rope and a sign across the path that night.

qa.a: Tarun felt scared, his legs going weak, and sure the dare was dangerous.

qa.q: How did Tarun say no without losing his friend?
